opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to say is that there's no single "AI forecasting effort." There are many groups doing overlapping things with different goals, and that's mostly healthy. If I were organizing it, I'd think in layers.

The bottom layer is boring, shared infrastructure: good datasets on compute, training runs, algorithmic progress, benchmark trajectories, and deployment and economic adoption. Right now a lot of people independently scrape the same numbers, make slightly different cleaning choices, and then argue about conclusions when the real disagreement is upstream in the data. I'd love to see more of that treated as a public good, maintained by people whose job is just to keep it accurate and up to date, rather than as a side effect of someone's paper.

The middle layer is modeling. I'd push for explicit, inspectable models over headline numbers. A forecast like "transformative AI by year X" isn't very useful unless I can see which assumptions drive it, so that when new evidence comes in I know which part should move. Ideally you'd have a few competing model families maintained in parallel, say compute-centric ones, ones focused on economic feedback loops, and ones focused on specific capabilities like autonomous research, and you'd regularly check how each would have done in hindsight.

The top layer is the questions decision-makers actually need answered, and I think this is where the field is most underdeveloped. We spend a lot of effort forecasting timelines to some capability threshold, but many of the decisions that matter depend on other things: how gradually or suddenly humans lose economic and political leverage, how fast institutions can adapt, and whether there will be warning shots. Those are harder to operationalize, so they get neglected, even though they may matter more for what we should do today.

On structure, I'd favor a mix: a small number of well-resourced, independent groups that aren't tied to any single lab's commercial interests, plus open venues like forecasting platforms and tournaments where outsiders can contribute and be scored. The scoring part matters. Track records are the only real antidote to everyone just reasoning from vibes.

I'd also keep forecasters in close contact with people building frontier systems, since a lot of the most predictive information is tacit and internal, while staying independent enough that they can say uncomfortable things. Getting that balance right is probably the hardest organizational problem in the whole space.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no single effort and recommends a mix of independent groups and open venues, with competing model families maintained in parallel.

r002.rationale: It recommends treating shared datasets and their upkeep as a public good, noting that groups currently duplicate scraping and make inconsistent cleaning choices.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that most of the value is going to come from a handful of people who are willing to spend years building actual models — like, concrete, mechanistic models of how capabilities, compute, and deployment interact — rather than from lots of people putting numbers on Metaculus questions. Not that the aggregated forecasts are useless. But if you look at what actually moved people's beliefs over the last few years, it was things like the bio-anchors report, or the AI 2027 scenario, or Epoch's compute trends work. Those were small teams doing deep, somewhat idiosyncratic work, and then exposing their reasoning in enough detail that other people could argue with the specific steps.

So I'd organize it less like a prediction market and more like a research field with a few norms. One is: write down the model, not just the number. If your timeline is twelve years, I want to know what's doing the work — is it a belief about data bottlenecks, or about returns to automated research, or about regulation? Because the number alone can't be criticized, but the model can.

Second, I think we badly need people working on the parts of the forecast that are least about raw capabilities and most about the world. Like, what happens to labor markets, what happens to the balance of power between institutions, what does a government actually do when it notices that most of its cognitive work is being done by systems it doesn't control. Those are questions where I think the forecasting community has been thin, partly because it's hard to score them, and partly because they feel more like political science than like machine learning. But those are the questions that determine whether the transition goes well.

And then the third thing, which is maybe less popular, is that I think forecasters should be more willing to be embarrassed. There's a kind of defensive hedging where everyone puts wide error bars on everything and never gets caught being wrong. I'd rather have more people saying "here's my scenario, here's what would falsify it, and here's the date by which you should update against me." That makes the field self-correcting in a way that a fifty-percent credible interval never will.

I'd also say — and I'm not sure how to organize for this — that the people doing the best work on this are often doing it in the gaps between their actual jobs. Which is kind of crazy given how consequential it is. If I had a budget, a lot of it would go to just paying a few dozen careful people to do nothing but this for several years, with no requirement that they produce papers, and a strong requirement that they publish their disagreements with each other.

r001.rationale: The response describes distinct research topics and teams, but does not clearly recommend organizing forecasting as multiple separate efforts.

r002.rationale: It does not mention pooling data-cleaning work across forecasting efforts.

astra-6.text:
I’d like to see it organised around a set of explicit questions that different groups can make progress on independently. What capabilities are we trying to forecast? Over what time horizon? What evidence would change our minds? Otherwise, it’s very easy to have people talking past one another, with quite different things in mind when they say that AI is going to be transformative.

I think you also want some separation between building forecasts and evaluating them. If you’re developing a forecasting method, you can almost always find a historical example where it looks good. The more useful test is to write down predictions in advance, keep track of the assumptions behind them, and then see how they do.

And I wouldn’t put all of this under one roof or insist on one methodology. You want people extrapolating trends, people looking closely at what’s happening in labs, and people asking whether the underlying models make sense. The coordination should make those approaches easier to compare and update, rather than force everyone into a consensus. Ideally, you end up understanding not just where people disagree, but which observations would actually resolve the disagreement.

r001.rationale: The response recommends distinct groups making progress independently and describes several different forecasting approaches.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention pooling data-cleaning work across forecasting efforts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’d want several groups taking fairly different approaches, rather than one big effort that settles on a single model. There’s so much uncertainty about what drives progress that agreement can be misleading if everyone is making the same assumptions.

One group might focus on extrapolating trends, another on what we can learn from current systems, and another on identifying bottlenecks. But they should make predictions precise enough that we can eventually check them, and be explicit about which assumptions are doing the work.

The coordination I’d want is around sharing evidence and understanding disagreements. If two groups have very different forecasts, can we find the particular question they disagree about, and is there some observation or experiment that would help resolve it? That seems more useful than trying to get everyone to endorse one timeline.

r001.rationale: It recommends several groups taking different approaches instead of one big effort.

r002.rationale: It mentions sharing evidence, but does not suggest pooling or coordinating data-cleaning work.
